questions.learning_objective: Prioritize synchronized cardioversion for wide-complex tachycardia with a pulse and cardiopulmonary compromise.
questions.stem: A 13-year-old hospitalized with myocarditis develops a regular wide-complex tachycardia. He has a pulse but is hypotensive, confused, and poorly perfused. What is the most appropriate immediate rhythm treatment?

options.text: Urgent synchronized cardioversion while resuscitation and expert support continue
Observation because ventricular tachycardia is often transient in myocarditis
Give adenosine first regardless of rhythm regularity or hemodynamic compromise
Start an oral beta-blocker and reassess later
Obtain CMR before treating the rhythm

questions.rationale: Wide-complex tachycardia with a pulse plus hypotension, altered mental status, or shock is an unstable tachyarrhythmia. Pediatric advanced life support prioritizes synchronized cardioversion rather than delayed pharmacologic or diagnostic maneuvers.

option_explanations.sync_cardio: Correct. Cardiopulmonary compromise changes the priority from rhythm diagnosis refinement to immediate electrical stabilization.
option_explanations.observe: Nonsustained asymptomatic ectopy may sometimes be monitored, but sustained wide-complex tachycardia with shock is immediately dangerous.
option_explanations.adenosine_any: Adenosine can have a diagnostic/therapeutic role in selected regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia without compromise, but unstable patients need synchronized cardioversion. Irregular wide-complex rhythms are particularly unsafe for indiscriminate adenosine use.
option_explanations.oral_beta: Oral therapy is too slow for an unstable rhythm and may worsen hemodynamics depending on the context.
option_explanations.wait_cmr: Imaging must not delay treatment of a life-threatening arrhythmia.

questions.board_pearl: In pediatric wide-complex tachycardia, hemodynamic stability determines urgency: compromise means synchronized cardioversion.

evidence.claim: Pediatric wide-complex tachycardia with cardiopulmonary compromise should be treated with synchronized cardioversion.

questions.learning_objective: Prioritize defibrillation and high-quality CPR when myocarditis deteriorates to a shockable cardiac-arrest rhythm.
questions.stem: A 10-year-old with fulminant myocarditis suddenly becomes unresponsive and pulseless. The monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the immediate priority?

options.text: Rapid defibrillation with high-quality CPR according to pediatric cardiac-arrest care
Give an antiarrhythmic medication before the first shock
Perform a complete echocardiogram before starting CPR
Confirm myocarditis by biopsy before treating the arrest
Use synchronized cardioversion because all ventricular rhythms should be synchronized

questions.rationale: VF and pulseless VT are shockable pediatric cardiac-arrest rhythms. Rapid defibrillation and high-quality CPR are the priority; myocarditis is the underlying cause, not a reason to delay standard resuscitation.

option_explanations.defib_cpr: Correct. Defibrillation is the definitive immediate treatment for VF/pulseless VT, with high-quality CPR minimizing no-flow time.
option_explanations.amio_first: Antiarrhythmics can be used in refractory shockable arrest, but they do not replace the priority of early defibrillation and CPR.
option_explanations.echo_first: Point-of-care echo may help identify reversible causes during arrest if it does not interrupt compressions, but it must not delay CPR or defibrillation.
option_explanations.biopsy_first: Etiologic confirmation has no role before treating cardiac arrest.
option_explanations.sync_cardio: Synchronized cardioversion is used for unstable tachycardia with a pulse. VF/pulseless VT requires unsynchronized defibrillation.

questions.board_pearl: Myocarditis changes the cause of arrest—not the first priorities of treating VF/pulseless VT.

evidence.claim: Rapid defibrillation is the priority for pediatric cardiac arrest with VF/pulseless VT.

questions.learning_objective: Apply the pediatric bradycardia sequence to complete AV block with cardiopulmonary compromise, including reversible-cause correction, resuscitative medications/CPR when indicated, and pacing preparation.
questions.stem: An 8-year-old with myocarditis develops complete AV block with dizziness, hypotension, and poor perfusion. Hypoxia and other immediately reversible contributors have been addressed, but the bradycardia and cardiopulmonary compromise persist. Which management sequence best matches current pediatric resuscitation principles?

options.text: Continue airway/oxygenation support and monitoring, treat the primary AV block with atropine when appropriate, give epinephrine and start CPR if the bradycardic low-output state meets resuscitation criteria, and prepare emergency pacing if compromise persists
Proceed directly to pacing as the only intervention and omit bradycardia resuscitation medications or CPR even if perfusion worsens
Give atropine, but if complete block and poor perfusion persist, defer further intervention while waiting to see whether the inflammatory block resolves spontaneously
Delay acute stabilization while arranging a permanent pacemaker because transient pacing has no role in myocarditis-related complete heart block
Base escalation primarily on the troponin trend and withhold rhythm-directed intervention if the myocardial injury marker is falling

questions.rationale: Complete AV block with cardiopulmonary compromise is a bradycardia emergency. Current pediatric resuscitation guidance combines correction of reversible contributors with atropine for primary AV conduction block, epinephrine and CPR when compromise persists and resuscitation criteria are met, and emergency pacing for refractory complete heart block.

option_explanations.pals_brady_sequence: Correct. Management is sequential and physiology-driven: support oxygenation/ventilation, address reversible causes, treat persistent compromised bradycardia, and escalate to pacing when complete block remains refractory.
option_explanations.pacing_only: Pacing may become necessary, but a child with ongoing cardiopulmonary compromise still needs simultaneous bradycardia resuscitation. Pacing is not a reason to omit support of airway, circulation, or CPR when indicated.
option_explanations.atropine_endpoint: Atropine can improve AV conduction in primary block, but persistent hypotension and poor perfusion require continued resuscitation rather than passive observation. Transient inflammatory block can recover, yet the child must remain perfused while recovery is awaited.
option_explanations.permanent_first: Some persistent high-grade block ultimately requires permanent pacing, but the immediate problem is unstable bradycardia. Temporary emergency pacing is specifically useful as a bridge when acute complete block does not respond to initial measures.
option_explanations.biomarker_strategy: Troponin reflects myocardial injury, not adequacy of AV conduction or perfusion. A falling troponin cannot override symptomatic complete heart block.

questions.board_pearl: In myocarditis-related complete heart block, treat the perfusing rhythm you have now while you determine whether conduction will recover later.

evidence.claim: For pediatric bradycardia with cardiopulmonary compromise due to primary AV block, atropine is recommended after reversible contributors such as hypoxia are addressed; persistent compromise may require epinephrine and CPR according to the bradycardia algorithm.
Emergency transcutaneous pacing may be considered for complete heart block with cardiopulmonary compromise unresponsive to initial resuscitative measures.

questions.learning_objective: Treat documented NSVT in active myocarditis as meaningful electrical instability even if the child is asymptomatic during the run.
questions.stem: A 7-year-old with myocarditis has a brief run of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia on telemetry but denies symptoms. Ventricular function is mildly depressed. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: It is evidence of electrical instability and supports continued monitored care and risk assessment
Because the run was asymptomatic and self-terminated, continue the same low-acuity plan without changing rhythm surveillance or risk assessment
Start chronic antiarrhythmic therapy solely because one brief NSVT run occurred, before defining recurrent burden or hemodynamic effect
Treat the event as telemetry artifact unless a second identical episode is captured, even though the stored tracing is consistent with ventricular tachycardia
Use absence of syncope during the run as evidence that early return to strenuous activity will be reasonable once resting EF normalizes

questions.rationale: Ventricular tachyarrhythmia is clinically significant in myocarditis even without symptoms and is associated with greater morbidity/resource use. The finding changes monitoring and follow-up risk assessment, but it does not by itself mandate one chronic antiarrhythmic strategy.

option_explanations.electrical_instability: Correct. Absence of symptoms during a short run does not make ventricular tachycardia benign in an inflamed myocardium; the finding should alter monitoring and risk assessment.
option_explanations.routine_floor: A self-terminating asymptomatic episode is less immediately unstable than sustained VT with shock, but true NSVT still supplies new electrical-risk information. Low-acuity observation without reassessment would under-react to the finding.
option_explanations.antiarrhythmic_now: Antiarrhythmic therapy may be appropriate for recurrent or clinically important ventricular arrhythmia, but one brief run should first be interpreted in the context of burden, ventricular function, hemodynamics, and specialist rhythm assessment.
option_explanations.artifact_default: Artifact is an important competing explanation for unusual telemetry, but the stem specifies a documented run. Once the tracing is verified as VT, it should not be dismissed until a recurrence occurs.
option_explanations.early_clearance: Syncope would increase concern, but absence of syncope does not establish electrical recovery. Return to strenuous activity after myocarditis depends on broader rhythm and recovery assessment.

questions.board_pearl: Asymptomatic ventricular tachycardia is still ventricular tachycardia; symptoms do not define electrical risk.

evidence.claim: Arrhythmias in pediatric myocarditis are associated with worse outcomes and greater resource utilization.
Ventricular arrhythmia is a high-risk feature in pediatric myocarditis.

questions.learning_objective: Pursue intermittent rhythm evaluation when syncope occurs despite a normal resting ECG in myocarditis.
questions.stem: An 11-year-old with suspected myocarditis has an episode of syncope. A resting ECG obtained afterward is unchanged from admission. Which next evaluation most directly addresses a dangerous intermittent cause?

options.text: Review continuous telemetry and obtain appropriate ambulatory/prolonged rhythm monitoring if needed
Repeat echocardiography first and stop the syncope workup if ventricular systolic function is unchanged
Prioritize repeat tissue-characterization CMR before reviewing telemetry because scar burden is the most direct test for a transient rhythm event
Complete an orthostatic/vasovagal evaluation and regard a compatible history as sufficient despite the active myocarditis context
Proceed directly to an invasive electrophysiology study before attempting to capture spontaneous intermittent rhythm abnormalities

questions.rationale: Intermittent tachy- or bradyarrhythmias may not appear on a resting ECG. Syncope in myocarditis is a high-risk symptom and warrants rhythm-focused evaluation and continued monitoring.

option_explanations.rhythm_monitor: Correct. Continuous or prolonged monitoring is designed to capture transient electrical events missed by a snapshot ECG.
option_explanations.repeat_echo: Echo is useful for ventricular function and hemodynamics, but unchanged systolic function does not exclude intermittent tachy- or bradyarrhythmia as the cause of syncope.
option_explanations.cmr_first: CMR can identify inflammation or scar that contributes to risk, but it does not directly capture a transient rhythm event. Rhythm review is the more direct next test for this question.
option_explanations.orthostatic_only: Vasovagal syncope remains common in children, but active myocarditis raises the pretest probability of a cardiac rhythm cause. A benign mechanism should not be accepted without adequate cardiac assessment.
option_explanations.ep_study: Invasive electrophysiology can be useful in selected arrhythmia problems, but spontaneous monitoring is less invasive and directly suited to detecting intermittent events before an invasive strategy is chosen.

questions.board_pearl: Syncope plus myocarditis is an intermittent-arrhythmia problem until an adequate rhythm evaluation says otherwise.

evidence.claim: Arrhythmic presentations including syncope are recognized myocarditis phenotypes and require risk stratification.
Myocarditis with arrhythmia or heart block warrants early ICU monitoring and therapy.

questions.learning_objective: Seek expert consultation before antiarrhythmic drug therapy for pediatric wide-complex tachycardia without cardiopulmonary compromise.
questions.stem: A 6-year-old with myocarditis has a regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia but remains alert, normotensive, and well perfused. Which general next-step principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Obtain expert consultation and define the rhythm before choosing antiarrhythmic therapy; selected regular monomorphic rhythms may allow diagnostic/therapeutic adenosine under appropriate monitoring
Perform synchronized cardioversion immediately despite preserved perfusion, before using the stability window for expert rhythm assessment
Begin empiric antiarrhythmic infusion before expert consultation because myocarditis makes ventricular tachycardia the presumed mechanism
Treat adenosine as the mandatory first step for every regular monomorphic wide-complex rhythm, independent of expert rhythm review
Presume supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy because the child is stable and manage it as a narrow-complex SVT pathway

questions.rationale: Stable pediatric wide-complex tachycardia has several possible mechanisms, and antiarrhythmic therapy can be proarrhythmic. Current pediatric guidance prioritizes expert consultation; adenosine may be useful only in selected regular monomorphic rhythms.

option_explanations.expert_stable_wct: Correct. Stability creates time for rhythm clarification and expert-guided therapy while the child remains closely monitored.
option_explanations.cardioversion_now: Synchronized cardioversion is appropriate when cardiopulmonary compromise is present and may be needed if stability deteriorates. In a currently stable child, expert rhythm assessment can guide a less reflexive approach.
option_explanations.empiric_amio: Ventricular tachycardia is a serious possibility, but stable wide-complex tachycardia can have several mechanisms and antiarrhythmics can carry hemodynamic/proarrhythmic risk. Expert-guided selection is preferred.
option_explanations.adenosine_mandatory: Adenosine can be useful in selected regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia, but it is not a universal first step and should be used within an appropriately monitored expert-informed pathway.
option_explanations.svt_assumption: SVT with aberrancy is a legitimate differential, but hemodynamic stability does not establish the mechanism. Treating a wide-complex rhythm as proven SVT before defining it can lead to inappropriate therapy.

questions.board_pearl: Stable wide-complex tachycardia buys time for expert rhythm definition—not for premature certainty about the mechanism.

evidence.claim: For pediatric wide-complex tachycardia without cardiopulmonary compromise, expert consultation is recommended before antiarrhythmic agents; adenosine may be useful when the rhythm is regular and monomorphic.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize that normalization of EF does not erase residual electrical risk.
questions.stem: A 15-year-old recovering from myocarditis has normal LV ejection fraction but frequent ventricular ectopy on ambulatory monitoring. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Mechanical recovery and electrical recovery are distinct; the ectopy requires continued cardiology assessment
If follow-up CMR shows resolution of edema, the frequent ectopy can be considered clinically unimportant despite its persistence
If the adolescent denies palpitations or syncope, normal EF is sufficient to treat the ambulatory ectopy as a benign recovery finding
Repeat troponin should determine whether the ectopy matters; a normal value would establish electrical recovery
Sports clearance can precede additional rhythm assessment because exercise testing after return will reveal whether the ectopy is clinically important

questions.rationale: Myocarditis recovery is multidimensional. Ventricular function can normalize while scar or electrical instability persists, so rhythm findings remain clinically relevant.

option_explanations.rhythm_independent: Correct. Function, symptoms, biomarkers, tissue findings, and rhythm do not necessarily recover at the same pace.
option_explanations.cmr_controls: Resolution of active edema is reassuring, but CMR and rhythm monitoring measure different recovery domains. Persistent frequent ectopy still requires direct electrical risk assessment.
option_explanations.symptom_controls: Absence of palpitations or syncope lowers symptomatic burden but does not make objectively frequent ventricular ectopy benign after myocarditis.
option_explanations.troponin_controls: Troponin reflects myocardial injury rather than rhythm stability. It may normalize while an arrhythmogenic substrate or ventricular ectopy persists.
option_explanations.exercise_after_clear: Exercise testing can be part of recovery assessment, but clinically important rhythm stability should be established before routine competitive clearance rather than tested only after return.

questions.board_pearl: A normal EF is not an electrical clearance test.

evidence.claim: Arrhythmia surveillance is part of myocarditis follow-up and return-to-activity assessment.
Persistent arrhythmic risk can remain after the acute inflammatory phase.

questions.concept: electrical risk independent of troponin trend
questions.learning_objective: Avoid using a falling troponin to de-escalate monitoring when conduction disease or arrhythmia persists.
questions.stem: A 12-year-old with myocarditis has a falling troponin concentration but intermittent second-degree/high-grade AV block continues on telemetry. What is the best management implication?

options.text: Continue monitored care because biomarker improvement does not establish electrical recovery
If blood pressure is currently normal between episodes, discharge with ambulatory monitoring and let the outpatient rhythm burden determine whether high-grade block matters
Use repeat CMR to decide whether telemetry can stop; absence of active edema would establish that the conduction abnormality is low risk
Place temporary pacing support for every intermittent high-grade block episode regardless of ventricular rate, symptoms, or perfusion
Continue telemetry only until troponin reaches the laboratory reference range, then de-escalate even if intermittent high-grade block remains

questions.rationale: Biomarkers and conduction-system recovery can follow different timelines. Persistent high-grade block remains a high-risk electrical finding even if the injury marker is improving.

option_explanations.continue_monitor: Correct. The active management problem is electrical stability, not simply biomarker direction.
option_explanations.ambulatory_discharge: Ambulatory monitoring is useful in selected stable follow-up settings, but persistent high-grade AV block during active myocarditis is a high-risk finding that warrants monitored specialist care before discharge decisions.
option_explanations.cmr_decides: CMR can clarify inflammation and scar but cannot substitute for direct rhythm assessment. Conduction instability may persist despite improvement in tissue markers.
option_explanations.pacing_all: Emergency pacing is considered when clinically significant bradycardia or complete block causes compromise and does not respond to initial measures. Intermittent block does not make pacing automatic in every circumstance.
option_explanations.troponin_threshold: A biomarker threshold cannot establish electrical recovery. High-grade block remains clinically relevant even when myocardial-injury markers improve or normalize.

questions.board_pearl: Do not let a better laboratory trend cancel an abnormal rhythm strip.

evidence.claim: Pediatric myocarditis with heart block warrants high-acuity monitoring and therapy.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize polymorphic ventricular tachycardia as an immediate life-threatening complication even when EF is preserved.
questions.stem: A 14-year-old with myocarditis has preserved LV systolic function but develops palpitations, near-syncope, and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia on telemetry. Which interpretation is most important?

options.text: This is potentially life-threatening electrical instability requiring urgent escalation regardless of preserved EF
Preserved EF allows CMR-based scar characterization to precede urgent rhythm escalation because global pump function is intact
If the episode self-terminates, begin outpatient antiarrhythmic planning and reassess the rhythm burden after discharge
Use monitored exercise testing to determine whether the polymorphic rhythm is reproducible before labeling it high risk
Normal global systolic function substantially lowers the immediate importance of the rhythm unless sustained hypotension develops

questions.rationale: Malignant ventricular arrhythmia can occur without severe global pump dysfunction. The immediate risk is electrical, and preserved EF does not protect against deterioration to cardiac arrest.

option_explanations.life_threatening: Correct. Near-syncope plus polymorphic VT is an acute escalation trigger.
option_explanations.cmr_first: CMR can contribute to later substrate assessment, but a malignant ventricular rhythm with near-syncope requires immediate electrical stabilization and monitoring rather than delayed escalation for imaging.
option_explanations.antiarrhythmic_outpatient: Self-termination does not make polymorphic VT with near-syncope an outpatient problem. Acute monitoring and specialist management are required before longer-term drug decisions.
option_explanations.exercise_provocation: Exercise testing may be useful during recovery in selected patients, but deliberately provoking a malignant rhythm during active myocarditis is not the next step.
option_explanations.ef_reassuring: EF measures global systolic performance and cannot exclude dangerous electrical instability. The rhythm is high risk even before sustained hypotension appears.

questions.board_pearl: Myocarditis can be electrically malignant even when the echocardiogram looks mechanically reassuring.

evidence.claim: Ventricular arrhythmias are major high-risk complications of pediatric myocarditis.
Arrhythmias in pediatric myocarditis are associated with increased morbidity/resource utilization.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize recurrent ventricular arrhythmia plus low-output physiology as a trigger for advanced-center/MCS escalation rather than treating rhythm and circulation as separate problems.
questions.stem: A 9-year-old with myocarditis has recurrent ventricular tachycardia despite initial rhythm treatment. Between episodes, ventricular function is severely depressed, lactate is rising, urine output is falling, and vasoactive needs are increasing. Which strategic response is best?

options.text: Treat the child as having combined electrical and pump instability and activate advanced heart-failure/MCS-level escalation now
Prioritize serial rhythm-suppression strategies first and reassess the low-output trajectory only after sustained rhythm control is achieved
Continue the current local ICU plan until another major vasoactive or organ-support threshold is crossed before involving an MCS-capable center
Defer advanced-center escalation until invasive ventilation or cardiac arrest occurs, because those events establish failure of conventional therapy
Obtain definitive local biopsy-based etiologic classification before activating MCS-level transfer so disease-specific therapy can be chosen first

questions.rationale: Recurrent malignant arrhythmia plus refractory low output is a high-risk pre-arrest myocarditis phenotype. Rhythm management, perfusion support, and advanced-center/MCS planning must occur in parallel.

option_explanations.combined_escalation: Correct. Electrical and mechanical instability amplify each other and should be managed as one deteriorating syndrome.
option_explanations.rhythm_sequence: Termination of VT may improve output, but severe ventricular dysfunction and worsening end-organ perfusion are independent threats. Waiting for complete rhythm control before escalating circulation support can lose the pre-arrest window.
option_explanations.local_threshold: Rising lactate, oliguria, severe dysfunction, recurrent VT, and increasing vasoactive needs already demonstrate a failing trajectory. Advanced-center involvement should occur before an arbitrary additional threshold is crossed.
option_explanations.airway_threshold: Invasive ventilation and arrest are late markers of deterioration, not prerequisites for transfer. Current pediatric guidance favors early MCS-capable-center escalation in refractory low output.
option_explanations.biopsy_before_mcs: Tissue diagnosis can change disease-specific treatment in selected high-risk myocarditis, but it should not delay stabilization or transfer when the child is developing refractory electrical and pump failure.

questions.board_pearl: When myocarditis is both electrically and mechanically unstable, escalation must address both domains simultaneously.

evidence.claim: Pediatric myocarditis with arrhythmia and refractory low cardiac output is a pre-arrest state in which early ICU and MCS-capable-center escalation is recommended/reasonable.
Fulminant myocarditis may require early mechanical circulatory support to prevent irreversible organ injury.
